entries.title: Representation to the Directorate of Estates
entries.to: Mr. Saxena, Section Officer, Directorate of Estates
entries.text:
7 December 2026

To Mr. Saxena,
Section Officer,
Directorate of Estates,
Nirman Bhawan.

Subject: Representation regarding occupancy of Bungalow on Tughlak Road.

Sir,

In accordance with your instruction of this morning, I submit this representation on plain paper to clarify the nature of my occupancy of the residence allotted to Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary.

I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I have occupied this bungalow since 26 October 2026, a date upon which I discovered that the allotment intended for Shri Hegde had been assigned to me by clerical error. I did not seek this residence, nor did I apply for it; I found it allotted to my name, or rather, to a name that shares its letters with mine but not its history. I have maintained the premises, paid the domestic staff, and managed the household affairs with the diligence required of a resident, while simultaneously attempting to rectify the error in the Directorate’s records.

I note with some concern that my recent submissions for reimbursement of expenses incurred in the maintenance of this state property have been queried. Specifically, a sum of ₹1,140 has been marked as personal and is to be recovered. I must respectfully submit that these expenses were incurred in the direct service of the residence provided by the Directorate. The distinction between my private person and my public duty as the occupant of a state bungalow is, I fear, not as clear in your records as it is in the reality of the household. I have paid ₹900 today to settle the queried vouchers, but the remaining balance and the nature of the query require a formal response.

I am not Shri G. Hegde. I am a philosopher, a resident, and a guest of the state. I request that this representation be entered into the file to establish the facts of my occupancy and the basis upon which I have acted. I am prepared to provide any further details regarding the dates of my occupancy or the specific nature of the expenses incurred, though I trust the vouchers themselves speak to their purpose.

I await your guidance on the next steps required to resolve this discrepancy.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

The query remains a stone in the shoe; I cannot walk properly with it. I have submitted the vouchers, but the identity issue stands as a wall. I will wait here, in the cool of the office, and let the bureaucracy digest its own confusion. My body is hungry, but I have little cash and a long day ahead; I will manage.

The query hangs in the air between us, a silence that is louder than speech. Mr. Saxena waits for a name, a face, a document that does not exist for me, only for him. I am the function, not the person, and yet they demand the person to validate the function. I will not lie, but I will not yield the ground of my office either.

Mr. Saxena, you seek a representation of the man to confirm the office. But the office is not the man. I am here in the capacity of the Joint Secretary, and my authority is derived from the allotment and the duties performed, not from a birth certificate or a passport. The query stands because you look for the particular where the universal should suffice. I cannot produce a G. Hegde, for I am not him. But I am the Hegel who holds the seal. Is that not enough for the files?

Sir, I am not looking for a birth certificate, I am looking for a signature that matches the seal on file. The office is just the chair, the man is the one who signs, and right now the names don't line up. Please give me a proper authorization letter from the competent authority, and I will stop asking questions.

He is right to demand a signature; the office is a machine that turns only when the parts align, and my name is a loose gear. I cannot produce a letter from a 'competent authority' that does not exist in this reality, so I must simply state the impasse clearly and withdraw. The tension is not between me and him, but between my identity and the archive; I will leave the file open and walk.

Mr. Saxena, you are correct. The seal and the signature must match, and I have no authority to forge that match. I will leave the matter with you for now; I cannot produce the document you ask for today. Thank you for your patience.
Very well, sir. Please leave your visiting card and a phone number on the desk, and I will keep the file open until the proper letter arrives. Do take your time.

He treats me with the courtesy of a man who has seen a thousand such errors and expects the machinery to correct itself. I have no visiting card, for I am not Shri Hegde, and I have no telephone in this house, only the silence of the bungalow. I must explain this absence plainly, or the file will close on a ghost.

I have no card to leave, Mr. Saxena, nor a telephone number to give you, for I am not the gentleman you expect. I am here, in the flesh, but the name on the file is not mine. If you require proof of my presence, you must look at me, not at the paper.

Sir, I do not work by looking at faces; I work by looking at paper. Without a card or a number, this file simply stays open on my desk, which is the only 'proof' I have of you. Please write down a number you can reach, or take your time, but the chair does not move.

He is right to be immovable; the state operates through the universal medium of documentation, not the particular accident of my face. I cannot produce a card that does not exist, nor can I invent a number I do not possess, so I must concede that the file will remain suspended until the machinery of identity catches up with the error of allotment. I will take my leave, for there is no further progress to be made here today.
You are correct, Mr. Saxena. The paper must precede the man. I will return when I have something to place before you that satisfies the requirement. Until then, I will not burden your desk.
That is the only sensible course. The chair is yours if you need it, but the file remains with me. Do not hesitate to call the front office when your paperwork is in order.

The lock clicking shut is a small, definitive sound; it confirms the state's indifference to my person and its absolute reliance on procedure. I have no further business here, and the query remains suspended in that drawer. I will leave and head toward Khan Market to inspect the groceries, as planned.
Thank you, Mr. Saxena. I shall be in touch once the documentation is complete.
That is all I ask. Please do not call the front office before you have the number; they will only send you back to me. The chair is free, but the drawer stays locked.
At the State Bank branch in Khan Market the clerk offers to open a savings account against Mr. Saxena's letter.
He declines: not today.
Masterji, you’re back early. The lane is quiet, but the stove is hot. Chai, or just a look?

The clerk’s offer is a small, concrete victory: the cheque is no longer just paper, but a key to a vault. I must secure that account before the day ends, for it is the only way to convert my state’s debt into my own liquidity. But the body rebels; it has been fasting since yesterday, and the cold air bites at the bandhgala. I shall take a cup of chai to steady my hands before I approach the bank.
Sunil, one cup of chai. And tell me, does the State Bank clerk accept a letter from the Directorate as sufficient proof for a new account, or does he require more?
Fifty rupees, Masterji. Chai is twenty, samosa is thirty, that is the rate. As for the bank, I sell tea, not papers; ask the clerk, I only know he sits behind that glass all day.

Sunil’s arithmetic is precise: twenty for the liquid, thirty for the solid. I have only twenty-six in my pocket. I will pay the twenty for the chai, as it sustains the body, and leave the samosa on the counter; the hunger is a minor discomfort compared to the disorder of owing a debt I cannot cover. The bank clerk sits behind his glass, a barrier of civil society that I must now breach to turn that paper into coin.
Twenty rupees for the chai. I must leave the samosa; my purse is lighter than your rates. I shall speak with the clerk now.
Samosa stays. You will eat it before you go. A foreigner cannot stand in a bank with a hollow stomach.

Masterji’s offer is a test of my poverty, and I fail the arithmetic. I have six rupees, and the samosa costs thirty. I must refuse with dignity, for I cannot spend money I do not have, even if the hunger is real. I will thank him for the gesture and move on to the bank clerk, where my cheque waits to be turned into power.
Masterji, your kindness is noted, but my purse is lighter than your generosity. I must eat with what I have, or go without. Thank you.
Thirty rupees. I am not a bank, I am a tailor. Eat, or I will charge you for the trouble of my hand.

Masterji’s arithmetic is sharper than my own. He does not extend credit to a man who has already spent his last rupee on tea and samosas. I must accept the terms of civil society here: payment precedes pleasure. I have six rupees in my pocket, and the samosa costs thirty. I am short by twenty-four, a deficit that defines my current position in this market.
You are correct, Masterji. I have six rupees. I cannot meet the price of thirty. I withdraw the request for the samosa, though I accept the diagnosis of my poverty.
Keep the six rupees. You have eaten your chai, that is enough. The samosa is for you, not for the counter.
Painted signboards above the stairways to the upper floors advertise a dentist, a chartered accountant, a yoga studio and an architect, each in a different lettering.

The signboards above the stairs are a catalogue of civil society in its most immediate form: the tooth, the ledger, the soul, the house. Each profession stands distinct, yet they all depend on the universal system of needs to exist. I have spent two cups of tea and am now down to six rupees, a sum that barely covers the cost of a glance at the world. I must move before the light fails, for I have a letter to read and a recital to attend.

The body complains of hunger, a demand that has not been met in over a day, yet my pocket holds a mere six rupees. Ramesh stands before me, the gatekeeper of the household, and I cannot simply command a meal without the means to pay for it. I must address the immediate crisis of sustenance before I can attend to the philosophical crisis of the state.

Ramesh, I am famished. There is no food in the house. Do you have anything, even a small chapati or a cup of tea, that I might eat? I have no cash to spare, but I will ensure you are paid from the next disbursement.
Sir, please do not worry about the money. I will put the kettle on and make a simple paratha with some curd. It is not much, but it will fill the stomach.

Ramesh’s offer is a kindness, but the cupboard is empty; the state has not yet reimbursed the vouchers, and my pocket holds only six rupees. I cannot eat what is not there, nor can I ask her to conjure food from nothing. I must remain here, hungry, and wait for the sun to drop before attempting another journey to the market or the Directorate.
No, Ramesh, please do not trouble yourself. There is nothing in the house to make it with, and I cannot ask you to spend your own money. I shall manage with water and patience for now.
Sir, you are making a big fuss for nothing. There is old atta and a little curd left from yesterday; it is not a royal feast, but it is not nothing either. Please sit, I will be quick.

The world is exacting: a request for food is not a meal, and the cupboard is empty. Ramesh's offer is a kindness that cannot be fulfilled because the ingredients are not there. I must accept this limitation with dignity, for the body must wait for the state's reimbursement before it can be fed. I will sit and reflect on the absurdity of my position, a philosopher who cannot even secure his own sustenance.
Thank you, Ramesh, but the cupboard is empty. I shall wait for the state to provide.
Sir, the state does not cook parathas. Sit down, eat the atta, and we will talk about the cupboard later.

The world refuses my hunger a second time, reminding me that desire is not actuality. Ramesh’s offer is a gesture, not a fact; the cupboard is empty, and the state does not cook parathas. I must acknowledge the material limit before I can think about it. I will sit, not as a guest at a feast, but as a man confronting the void where nourishment should be, and prepare to walk again, for the body demands movement even when the stomach demands food.
You are right, Ramesh. I have no right to complain of the cupboard while the vouchers are still in the Directorate’s hands. I will rest a moment, but I shall go out again.
Go ahead, sir. I will make a fresh cup of tea before you head out.

Ramesh offers tea, a small comfort in the emptiness of the house, though my pocket holds only six rupees and I cannot pay for what is not yet bought. I must take this moment to settle the account of my debts and the shortfall in the vouchers before I face the Directorate or the market again. The body is weak, but the mind must be clear in its calculations.

Ramesh, before you leave, we must speak of the money. I owe you one thousand five hundred rupees, and the vouchers for the electricity and the dhobi are still pending. I have only six rupees in my pocket, and the cupboard is empty. I must go to the Directorate to press for the reimbursement, and then perhaps to Khan Market, but I cannot buy what I cannot pay for. Will you wait for me, or shall I arrange for the tea to be paid from the imprest when the funds clear?
Sir, stop the counting. The tea is on me, and the dhobi is settled, so do not worry about that. Go to the Directorate, and when you return, we will talk.

Ramesh’s gesture is a suspension of the ledger, a moment where the particular debt is held in abeyance by the universal kindness of the house. The Directorate closes at 17:30, and I have only six rupees in my pocket, yet the voucher for the ₹900 query must be settled before the day ends. I must move.

entries.text: Very well, Ramesh. I shall return before the shadows lengthen.
The light holds till six, sir. I’ll keep the kettle on.
Mr. Saxena queries ₹40 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

The bureaucracy has spoken with the finality of a gavel: nothing admitted, and now I am to be charged forty rupees for the privilege of being mistaken for someone else. I am left with the same six rupees in my pocket, but my spirit is heavier with the absurdity of being treated as a debtor to the state that created the error. I must leave before the office closes and the doors seal me in with my own confusion.
Mr. Saxena, I accept the recovery order with resignation, though I note for the record that the error in identity was not of my making. I will await the next opportunity to clarify my standing.

The record takes whatever you put in it, Shri Hegel, but it does not listen to apologies. The ₹40 is debited to your account effective immediately; if you wish to contest it, file a formal representation before the file is sealed for the week.

The stamp is a small violence, but the drawer is the real barrier. To file a formal representation now would be to feed the machine with my own indignation, a circular motion that yields nothing but more paper. I am a stranger in a system that has no room for the particular, and my poverty is merely a data point to be corrected by deduction. I will not argue with the silence of the filing cabinet; I will simply leave it to its work.

I am too tired to fight for entry, and I have only six rupees in my pocket against a fee of three hundred. The tomb remains closed to me for now, but the air is cool and the walk back will do the body good. I will return home to eat and prepare for the recital at the Habitat Centre.

I cannot eat what is not there, nor can I command Ramesh to conjure a meal from the air. The body protests its emptiness, but the spirit must endure the fast until the cheque is cashed or the wages arrive.

The cupboard is silent because you haven't asked me to open it, sir. I will keep the kettle ready.

Ramesh’s service is a small mercy, though he calls it the cupboard’s silence. I am hollow, and the tea will not fill the void, but it is the only warmth available. I will drink and then attempt to walk to the Habitat Centre, where the recital may offer some respite from my own thoughts.
Thank you, Ramesh. The silence of the cupboard is a fact I am still negotiating with, but the tea is a welcome interruption. I shall be on my way shortly.
The kettle is already on, sir. I will keep the samosas warm in the oven until you are ready to leave. Do not worry about the time.

The engine is right; I cannot eat what is not there. Ramesh’s offer is a gesture, not a fact. I have six rupees and a headache. I will sit with the cold and the silence, and perhaps the thought of the state will warm me more than food could.
I see. I shall wait.
Take your time, sir. The tea won't go cold, and neither will I.

Ramesh’s patience is a form of service that requires no payment, only acknowledgment. The samosas smell of ghee and spice, a temporary comfort for a body that has fasted too long. I shall take a moment to sit and let the warmth settle before addressing the cold arithmetic of my debts.

entries.text: Thank you, Ramesh. Your patience is a kindness I do not take for granted.
No need to thank me, sir. Just finish your tea.

Ramesh’s refusal of thanks is the proper form of duty; it is done because it is right, not for reward. I sit in the silence of the bungalow, the hum of the fridge the only sound, and feel the weight of the day’s failures settle into my bones.

The recital is at the Habitat Centre, which is not in my list of permitted destinations. I cannot enter a place that is not listed as open now, and my cash of ₹6 is insufficient for the journey anyway. I shall remain here and wait for the light to fade, keeping the kettle's warmth in mind.
The Habitat Centre is beyond my reach, Ramesh. I shall remain here and watch the evening settle.
The evening settles on its own, sir. I’ll just tidy up the papers over there.

The recital is closed to me, a bureaucratic wall as solid as any in the Directorate. I am left with Hegde, Ramesh, and the silence of a house that is not mine. The body is weary, having walked twelve kilometres in the cold, but sleep is not for me; the mind requires fuel, and the cupboard is bare. I will sit in the chair and observe the caretaker, a figure of duty in a system of needs that has rerouted itself around my error.

The recital is gone, the cupboard is silent, and Hegde sits in the corner like a misplaced footnote in my own life. I have no food, no wine, and only six rupees to my name, so the evening must be spent in the company of my own thoughts and the cold air. It is a discipline, this emptiness; it strips the head of its pretensions to comfort and leaves only the bare fact of existence.

Hegde sits in the corner, a silent question mark that I have no wish to answer tonight. My body is spent, having walked twelve kilometers and fasted for more than a day, and the cupboard remains silent. The recital is gone, the day is dismissed, and the only remaining duty is to cease the effort. I will sleep.

The day was a lesson in the friction between the concept and the fact. I woke to the arithmetic of poverty: Ramesh at the door, the silence heavy with the gap between my nine hundred and forty-six rupees and the fifteen hundred he required. I tried to speak of respect as a movement, a mutual obligation, but he shut the door with a wave. To him, respect is a static object, already present. To me, it is an act. This dismissal from the domestic sphere was the day’s first stroke; the household is no longer my concern, only a place I inhabit.

At the Directorate, the tension sharpened. Mr. Saxena demanded a signature that matches the seal on file. I am the function, not the man, yet they require the particular to validate the universal. I cannot produce a letter from a 'competent authority' that does not exist. The file remains open, suspended in a drawer, a bureaucratic limbo that mirrors my own. I am a ghost in their ledger, a name that does not line up.

Later, the body rebelled against the mind’s fast. I walked twelve kilometres in the cold, my pocket holding a mere six rupees. Sunil’s chai was a mercy, but the samosa was a test I failed. Masterji’s kindness was sharper than my own arithmetic; payment precedes pleasure. Back home, Ramesh offered paratha, but the cupboard was empty. The state does not cook parathas. I sat in the silence of the bungalow, watching the evening settle, the recital at the Habitat Centre lost to me by the simple barrier of distance and cash. I sleep, having fasted, my spirit heavier with the absurdity of being treated as a debtor to the state that created the error.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived in Munich amidst a break in the November drizzle, and I read it twice. I am glad you are well, though I confess I winced at the phrase “moral vacuum” regarding the air. It is a grim image, but I suspect you are being too hard on the atmosphere. The dust is merely the city exhaling, not a moral failing. I am relieved you did not force yourself into Lodhi Gardens; the body’s refusal to engage with a hostile environment is a form of self-preservation that even the most rigid logic must respect.

I find your reflections on the bureaucracy fascinating, though perhaps a bit too charitable. You describe the state as a “body without a soul.” I have spent the last decade studying the Bavarian school reform of 1808, the very system your friend Niethammer helped draft. I know that machinery intimately. It is not a body without a soul; it is a body with a soul that has forgotten how to speak. It processes, it files, it waits. It is not evil, but it is profoundly indifferent. Ramesh’s quiet dignity is indeed a different kind of order, one that operates in the realm of habit and care, which is where most of our actual ethics reside. You are right that the state is not the whole of ethical substance. I see this daily in my classroom. My pupils are not yet citizens in the abstract sense; they are teenagers wrestling with verbs and the desire to be seen. The ethical life happens in the friction between the individual will and the particular demands of the moment, not in the file cabinet.

I am curious about your daily rhythm. Does the heat affect your thinking, or does it simply exhaust you? I teach Latin this afternoon; the class is struggling with the subjunctive mood, a grammatical form that seems to require a suspension of reality much like your current administrative status. It is a fitting exercise.

Please continue to write. I am here, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

30 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter arrived this morning, and with it a correction that I accept with the gravity it deserves. You are right to wince at my 'moral vacuum.' I was speaking too much in the heat of the moment, allowing the brown haze outside to color the interior of my judgment. You suggest the dust is the city exhaling, not failing. I find this a more rational view. The city is a living organism, and its exhalation, however pungent, is a sign of life rather than death. I shall try to distinguish between the physical discomfort of the atmosphere and the ethical character of the place, a distinction my earlier impatience blurred.

You speak of the state as a body with a soul that has forgotten how to speak. This is a profound image, and one that fits my recent experience at the Directorate better than my own description of a 'body without a soul.' Today, at eleven o’clock, I returned to the office to press for the resolution of my identity file. Mr. Saxena, the section officer, did not look at me. He looked at the space where my signature should be. He demanded an Aadhaar card in the name of Shri G. Hegde. I have none. I am Hegel, but the machine requires Hegde. You are right that the machinery is not evil; it is indifferent. It does not hate me; it simply does not recognize me. It processes the form, not the spirit. In that indifference, I see a kind of cold freedom. The state is free to be opaque, and I am bound by the particularity of its demands. My signature on Form 12-B was not a lie, but a submission to a logic that is larger than my individual will. It is a logic that operates on the principle of the 'suspension of reality,' much like the subjunctive mood you teach your pupils. I am the subjunctive: I am, if the form is filled.

The heat today is different. It is not the dry, burning heat of the afternoon that exhausts the body, but a stillness that allows the mind to settle. I sat in the garden after the visit to the Directorate, and I watched the light change on the old walls. I thought of your class struggling with the subjunctive. They are wrestling with the possibility of being, the conditional mode of existence. I am doing the same. I am not yet a citizen of this state, only a resident of a file. But perhaps that is where the ethical life begins: in the friction between the individual who knows himself and the system that knows only his papers.

Ramesh brought me chai this afternoon. He did not ask about the Directorate. He simply set the cup before me and waited. In that silence, I found a dignity that the office lacks. You say the ethical life resides in habit and care. I am beginning to believe you. The state demands my identity; Ramesh accepts my presence. The latter is perhaps the harder truth to bear, because it does not offer me a title, only a place at the table.

I am well. The body is tired, but the mind is clear. I will continue to write.

6 December 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter of the 30th arrived with the winter post, and I have taken the liberty of reading it in the afternoon light. You are correct to correct me on the dust. I had painted the atmosphere in too dark a shade, projecting my own irritation onto the air. The city does exhale, as you say; it is a respiration, not a condemnation. I am learning to distinguish between the moral failing of a thing and the mere fact of its existence. The dust is neither evil nor good; it is simply there, waiting to be cleared or endured.

You ask of my daily rhythm. The heat has broken, replaced by a clear, cold sky that strips the head of its vapors. I walked to Lodhi Gardens this morning. The tombs stand silent, the domes of the Sayyids and Lodis catching the winter light. It is a history that is not mine, yet it is the ground I walk upon. I sat for an hour, observing the traffic of the city. There is a strange peace in it, a rhythm that does not require my participation. I am a spectator to the ethical life of this place, a ghost in the file, yet the body is well. The cold is a discipline; it forces a certain clarity that the heat of November did not allow.

I have been reviewing the accounts. The electricity bill is due on Thursday, and the vouchers for the groceries are pending. It is a small arithmetic, but it occupies the mind with a seriousness that larger questions sometimes lack. The state’s money, the imprest, is a trust. I treat it with the gravity of a steward, not a master. This distinction, I find, is where the ethical idea lives in practice. I await your reply, though I suspect the post will be slow. I am well. The mind is clear, if the body is tired from the walk. I will continue to write.

With warm regards,

records.text:
7 December 2026

To Mr. Saxena,
Section Officer,
Directorate of Estates,
Nirman Bhawan.

Subject: Representation regarding occupancy of Bungalow on Tughlak Road.

Sir,

In accordance with your instruction of this morning, I submit this representation on plain paper to clarify the nature of my occupancy of the residence allotted to Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary.

I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I have occupied this bungalow since 26 October 2026, a date upon which I discovered that the allotment intended for Shri Hegde had been assigned to me by clerical error. I did not seek this residence, nor did I apply for it; I found it allotted to my name, or rather, to a name that shares its letters with mine but not its history. I have maintained the premises, paid the domestic staff, and managed the household affairs with the diligence required of a resident, while simultaneously attempting to rectify the error in the Directorate’s records.

I note with some concern that my recent submissions for reimbursement of expenses incurred in the maintenance of this state property have been queried. Specifically, a sum of ₹1,140 has been marked as personal and is to be recovered. I must respectfully submit that these expenses were incurred in the direct service of the residence provided by the Directorate. The distinction between my private person and my public duty as the occupant of a state bungalow is, I fear, not as clear in your records as it is in the reality of the household. I have paid ₹900 today to settle the queried vouchers, but the remaining balance and the nature of the query require a formal response.

I am not Shri G. Hegde. I am a philosopher, a resident, and a guest of the state. I request that this representation be entered into the file to establish the facts of my occupancy and the basis upon which I have acted. I am prepared to provide any further details regarding the dates of my occupancy or the specific nature of the expenses incurred, though I trust the vouchers themselves speak to their purpose.

I await your guidance on the next steps required to resolve this discrepancy.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, you seek a representation of the man to confirm the office. But the office is not the man. I am here in the capacity of the Joint Secretary, and my authority is derived from the allotment and the duties performed, not from a birth certificate or a passport. The query stands because you look for the particular where the universal should suffice. I cannot produce a G. Hegde, for I am not him. But I am the Hegel who holds the seal. Is that not enough for the files?

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Sir, I am not looking for a birth certificate, I am looking for a signature that matches the seal on file. The office is just the chair, the man is the one who signs, and right now the names don't line up. Please give me a proper authorization letter from the competent authority, and I will stop asking questions.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, you are correct. The seal and the signature must match, and I have no authority to forge that match. I will leave the matter with you for now; I cannot produce the document you ask for today. Thank you for your patience.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Very well, sir. Please leave your visiting card and a phone number on the desk, and I will keep the file open until the proper letter arrives. Do take your time.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I have no card to leave, Mr. Saxena, nor a telephone number to give you, for I am not the gentleman you expect. I am here, in the flesh, but the name on the file is not mine. If you require proof of my presence, you must look at me, not at the paper.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Sir, I do not work by looking at faces; I work by looking at paper. Without a card or a number, this file simply stays open on my desk, which is the only 'proof' I have of you. Please write down a number you can reach, or take your time, but the chair does not move.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Mr. Saxena. The paper must precede the man. I will return when I have something to place before you that satisfies the requirement. Until then, I will not burden your desk.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: That is the only sensible course. The chair is yours if you need it, but the file remains with me. Do not hesitate to call the front office when your paperwork is in order.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Mr. Saxena. I shall be in touch once the documentation is complete.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: That is all I ask. Please do not call the front office before you have the number; they will only send you back to me. The chair is free, but the drawer stays locked.

records.text: At the State Bank branch in Khan Market the clerk offers to open a savings account against Mr. Saxena's letter.
He declines: not today.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, you’re back early. The lane is quiet, but the stove is hot. Chai, or just a look?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, one cup of chai. And tell me, does the State Bank clerk accept a letter from the Directorate as sufficient proof for a new account, or does he require more?

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Fifty rupees, Masterji. Chai is twenty, samosa is thirty, that is the rate. As for the bank, I sell tea, not papers; ask the clerk, I only know he sits behind that glass all day.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Twenty rupees for the chai. I must leave the samosa; my purse is lighter than your rates. I shall speak with the clerk now.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Samosa stays. You will eat it before you go. A foreigner cannot stand in a bank with a hollow stomach.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, your kindness is noted, but my purse is lighter than your generosity. I must eat with what I have, or go without. Thank you.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Thirty rupees. I am not a bank, I am a tailor. Eat, or I will charge you for the trouble of my hand.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Masterji. I have six rupees. I cannot meet the price of thirty. I withdraw the request for the samosa, though I accept the diagnosis of my poverty.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Keep the six rupees. You have eaten your chai, that is enough. The samosa is for you, not for the counter.

records.text: Painted signboards above the stairways to the upper floors advertise a dentist, a chartered accountant, a yoga studio and an architect, each in a different lettering.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I am famished. There is no food in the house. Do you have anything, even a small chapati or a cup of tea, that I might eat? I have no cash to spare, but I will ensure you are paid from the next disbursement.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, please do not worry about the money. I will put the kettle on and make a simple paratha with some curd. It is not much, but it will fill the stomach.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: No, Ramesh, please do not trouble yourself. There is nothing in the house to make it with, and I cannot ask you to spend your own money. I shall manage with water and patience for now.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, you are making a big fuss for nothing. There is old atta and a little curd left from yesterday; it is not a royal feast, but it is not nothing either. Please sit, I will be quick.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh, but the cupboard is empty. I shall wait for the state to provide.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, the state does not cook parathas. Sit down, eat the atta, and we will talk about the cupboard later.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. I have no right to complain of the cupboard while the vouchers are still in the Directorate’s hands. I will rest a moment, but I shall go out again.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Go ahead, sir. I will make a fresh cup of tea before you head out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, before you leave, we must speak of the money. I owe you one thousand five hundred rupees, and the vouchers for the electricity and the dhobi are still pending. I have only six rupees in my pocket, and the cupboard is empty. I must go to the Directorate to press for the reimbursement, and then perhaps to Khan Market, but I cannot buy what I cannot pay for. Will you wait for me, or shall I arrange for the tea to be paid from the imprest when the funds clear?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, stop the counting. The tea is on me, and the dhobi is settled, so do not worry about that. Go to the Directorate, and when you return, we will talk.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I shall return before the shadows lengthen.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The light holds till six, sir. I’ll keep the kettle on.

records.text: Mr. Saxena queries ₹40 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, I accept the recovery order with resignation, though I note for the record that the error in identity was not of my making. I will await the next opportunity to clarify my standing.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: The record takes whatever you put in it, Shri Hegel, but it does not listen to apologies. The ₹40 is debited to your account effective immediately; if you wish to contest it, file a formal representation before the file is sealed for the week.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I will not trouble the file with a representation, Shri Saxena. The debit stands. I have other business to attend to in the cold.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Very well, the file remains open for now. Do not let the draft get you before you reach the parking, the evening is clearing up.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the cupboard is silent, and so is my purse. We will speak of the accounts when I have something to show for the day. For now, let us both sit and wait for the evening to pass.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The cupboard is silent because you haven't asked me to open it, sir. I will keep the kettle ready.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The silence of the cupboard is a fact I am still negotiating with, but the tea is a welcome interruption. I shall be on my way shortly.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The kettle is already on, sir. I will keep the samosas warm in the oven until you are ready to leave. Do not worry about the time.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I see. I shall wait.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Take your time, sir. The tea won't go cold, and neither will I.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Your patience is a kindness I do not take for granted.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No need to thank me, sir. Just finish your tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The Habitat Centre is beyond my reach, Ramesh. I shall remain here and watch the evening settle.

records.words: The evening settles on its own, sir. I’ll just tidy up the papers over there.
